title: What are streaming trigger modes — `processingTime("30 seconds")` (fixed interval micro-batches), `once()` (single batch then stop), `availableNow()` (process all available data then stop, good for cost-saving), `continuous("1 second")` (experimental true continuous) — and how do you control input rate (`maxOffsetsPerTrigger`, `maxFilesPerTrigger`)?
shortTitle: Streaming trigger modes and input-rate control

s1_definition.profdef: A trigger in Structured Streaming defines when and how often a query runs a micro-batch. `processingTime("30 seconds")` runs a batch at a fixed wall-clock interval. `once()` runs exactly one batch over whatever data is available and then stops, suited to scheduled jobs. `availableNow()` processes all currently available data, possibly over several micro-batches, then stops, which is the modern cost-saving replacement for `once()` because it respects rate limits. `continuous("1 second")` is an experimental true continuous mode with millisecond latency and limited operation support. Input rate is controlled independently with source options such as `maxOffsetsPerTrigger` for Kafka, which caps records read per trigger, and `maxFilesPerTrigger` for file sources, which caps files read per trigger, both acting as back-pressure to keep each batch a manageable size.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India the trigger is the schedule on which the clerk processes the incoming transaction tray. Fixed-interval is "process the tray every thirty seconds." Once is "process whatever is in the tray right now, then go home" — a nightly run. Available-now is "clear the whole tray in as many passes as needed, respecting how many slips you may handle per pass, then go home" — a smarter nightly run that does not choke on a huge backlog. Continuous is "never stop, process each slip the instant it lands," used rarely for ultra-low latency. The rate controls are the rule "handle at most ten thousand slips per pass" so no single pass overwhelms the clerk.
s1_definition.oneliner: processingTime runs batches at a fixed interval, once runs one batch then stops, availableNow drains all data in rate-limited batches then stops, continuous is experimental low-latency — and maxOffsetsPerTrigger / maxFilesPerTrigger cap how much each batch ingests.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A trigger in Structured Streaming defines when and how often a query runs a micro-batch. `processingTime("30 seconds")` runs a batch at a fixed wall-clock interval. `once()` runs exactly one batch over whatever data is available and then stops, suited to scheduled jobs. `availableNow()` processes all currently available data, possibly over several micro-batches, then stops, which is the modern cost-saving replacement for `once()` because it respects rate limits. `continuous("1 second")` is an experimental true continuous mode with millisecond latency and limited operation support. Input rate is controlled independently with source options such as `maxOffsetsPerTrigger` for Kafka, which caps records read per trigger, and `maxFilesPerTrigger` for file sources, which caps files read per trigger, both acting as back-pressure to keep each batch a manageable size.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India the trigger is the schedule on which the clerk processes the incoming transaction tray. Fixed-interval is "process the tray every thirty seconds." Once is "process whatever is in the tray right now, then go home" — a nightly run. Available-now is "clear the whole tray in as many passes as needed, respecting how many slips you may handle per pass, then go home" — a smarter nightly run that does not choke on a huge backlog. Continuous is "never stop, process each slip the instant it lands," used rarely for ultra-low latency. The rate controls are the rule "handle at most ten thousand slips per pass" so no single pass overwhelms the clerk.

**One line to remember:** processingTime runs batches at a fixed interval, once runs one batch then stops, availableNow drains all data in rate-limited batches then stops, continuous is experimental low-latency — and maxOffsetsPerTrigger / maxFilesPerTrigger cap how much each batch ingests.

sections.s2_technical:
The default trigger, when you specify none, runs micro-batches back to back: as soon as one batch finishes, the next starts if data is available. This gives the lowest micro-batch latency but can produce very frequent, tiny batches. You set an explicit trigger with `writeStream.trigger(...)` to control cadence.

`Trigger.ProcessingTime("30 seconds")` runs a batch every thirty seconds of wall-clock time. If a batch finishes early, Spark waits until the interval elapses; if a batch overruns the interval, the next starts immediately after. This is the standard production trigger for steady, predictable streaming because it bounds how often you write to the sink and interact with the state store.

`Trigger.Once()` runs a single micro-batch over all available data and stops. It was used for scheduled incremental jobs — spin up a cluster, process the new data once, shut down to save cost. Its weakness is that it ignores `maxOffsetsPerTrigger`, so a large backlog is processed in one giant batch that can blow up memory. `Trigger.AvailableNow()` is the modern replacement: it also processes all available data and stops, but it does so across multiple micro-batches that respect the rate limits, so a huge backlog is drained safely in bounded chunks. For periodic batch-like runs on streaming sources, availableNow is now preferred.

`Trigger.Continuous("1 second")` is the experimental continuous processing mode that aims for millisecond end-to-end latency by running long-lived tasks instead of micro-batches, checkpointing at the given interval. It supports only a limited set of operations — basically map-like transformations and simple selects, not arbitrary aggregations or joins — so it is rarely used in production. Micro-batch mode remains the robust default.

Input-rate control is separate from the trigger and is set on the source. For Kafka, `maxOffsetsPerTrigger` caps the total number of records read across all partitions per trigger, which is the primary back-pressure knob; for file sources, `maxFilesPerTrigger` caps how many new files are picked up per trigger, and there is also `maxBytesPerTrigger` in newer versions. These prevent a single batch from ingesting a massive backlog, which would cause long batch durations, memory pressure, and sink timeouts. A senior-level nuance is that rate limits and triggers work together: with availableNow plus maxOffsetsPerTrigger, a terabyte backlog is drained in many bounded batches and then the job stops cleanly, which is the pattern for cost-efficient scheduled streaming on a backlog, whereas processingTime plus a rate limit is the pattern for steady live processing that never falls hopelessly behind.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a live fraud-scoring stream that must process transactions every thirty seconds predictably. This is the processingTime trigger.

Problem 2 — A nightly reconciliation job must drain the entire day's backlog from the transactions topic and then stop to release the cluster, without choking on the backlog size. This is availableNow with a per-trigger rate limit, superior to once.

Problem 3 — Each batch must not ingest more than a safe number of records so batch duration stays bounded. This is maxOffsetsPerTrigger as back-pressure.

The demo simulates a backlog and shows how a once-style single batch would ingest everything at once, while an availableNow-style run with a per-trigger cap drains the same backlog in several bounded batches, logging each batch size.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a backlog of twenty-five thousand records on the transactions source, and a per-trigger cap of ten thousand.

Step 1: The once-style run executes. It takes the entire backlog in a single batch, ingesting all twenty-five thousand records at once and ignoring the rate limit. This is logged as a warning because such a giant batch risks memory pressure.

Step 2: The available-now-style run executes against a fresh twenty-five-thousand backlog. The first batch takes ten thousand, the cap.

Step 3: The second batch takes another ten thousand, leaving five thousand.

Step 4: The third batch takes the final five thousand, the backlog is empty, and the job stops. The same backlog is drained safely in three bounded batches instead of one dangerous batch, demonstrating why availableNow plus a rate limit is preferred for backlog draining.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 05:21:00 INFO    === once(): 25000 record backlog ===
2026-10-30 05:21:00 WARNING once(): single batch ingested 25000 records (rate limit ignored)
2026-10-30 05:21:00 INFO    === availableNow() with cap 10000: same 25000 backlog ===
2026-10-30 05:21:00 INFO    availableNow(): batch ingested 10000 records (cap 10000)
2026-10-30 05:21:00 INFO    availableNow(): batch ingested 10000 records (cap 10000)
2026-10-30 05:21:00 INFO    availableNow(): batch ingested 5000 records (cap 10000)
2026-10-30 05:21:00 INFO    availableNow(): drained in 3 batches, then stop
2026-10-30 05:21:00 INFO    Trigger modes demo complete.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A trigger in Structured Streaming controls when and how often a query runs a micro-batch. ProcessingTime with a fixed interval runs a batch on that wall-clock cadence and is the standard production trigger for steady live streaming. Once runs a single batch over all available data and stops, which was used for scheduled incremental jobs, but its weakness is that it ignores the per-trigger rate limit, so a large backlog becomes one giant batch. AvailableNow is the modern replacement: it also drains all available data and stops, but across multiple rate-limited micro-batches, so a huge backlog is processed safely in bounded chunks. Continuous mode is experimental, aims for millisecond latency with long-lived tasks, supports only simple operations, and is rarely used in production.

Input rate is controlled separately on the source, independent of the trigger. For Kafka, maxOffsetsPerTrigger caps the total records read per trigger and is the main back-pressure knob; for file sources, maxFilesPerTrigger caps files per trigger, and newer versions add maxBytesPerTrigger. These keep each batch a manageable size so batch duration, memory, and sink interaction stay bounded. The key insight is that triggers and rate limits work together: availableNow plus a rate limit drains a backlog cost-efficiently and then stops, while processingTime plus a rate limit keeps live processing steady and prevents the job from falling hopelessly behind.

At the National Bank of India I used processingTime of thirty seconds with a ten-thousand record per-trigger cap for a live fraud-scoring stream, which gave predictable cadence and bounded batches. For the nightly reconciliation I used availableNow with the same rate limit, so it drained the entire day's backlog in several safe batches and then stopped to release the cluster, which was far better than once because once would have tried to ingest the whole backlog in a single batch. In interviews I summarize it as: processingTime for steady live cadence, availableNow for cost-saving backlog draining that respects rate limits, once as its older less-safe cousin, continuous only for experimental ultra-low latency, and maxOffsetsPerTrigger or maxFilesPerTrigger as the back-pressure that keeps every batch bounded.
